text:
Cognitive Warning: As you de-armor, you will feel more naked and exposed than you're used to, and you'll assume everyone can see your anxiety, when really they notice far less of it than you think (Dr. Nicholas Epley calls this the "Illusion of Transparency" in his book Mindwise).

You'll also feel like people are judging you, when they're mostly just thinking about themselves, because an armored brain reads its own threat level into neutral faces. So during this protocol, do not trust your social intuition. A racing heart means your reasoning brain is offline (see the "Metabolic Red Line" below), so assume you are misreading every room, at least until your heart rate is back down to your usual resting rate, and under 90 BPM.
section: A Complete Guide to Bio-De-Armoring, the warnings at the top: the Cognitive Warning; A Complete Guide to Bio-De-Armoring, the warnings at the top: the second paragraph of the Cognitive Warning
reader: an adult with trauma or an addiction who has read the short introduction and is reading the warnings before starting the protocol, who often feels judged in a room

questions.Q1: PASS: each sentence opens on its point
questions.Q2: PASS: each instruction says what it is for in the reader's terms (why not to start them, what to stop for)
questions.Q3: PASS: each thing is named exactly
questions.Q4: PASS: each unfamiliar term is said in plain words where it is first used
questions.Q5: PASS: each "and", "so" and "but" turns on the clause before it
questions.Q6: PASS: the claim, then what the evidence shows, then its limit
questions.Q7: PASS: each fact is about the reader's own symptom or the tool they are deciding on
questions.Q8: N/A: no group or list inside this paragraph
questions.Q9: PASS: one step a clause, with the small words that carry the relation kept

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
